title: Distributions
summary: Histograms, the normal curve, skew and z-scores.

steps.title: The shape of the data
body: A **distribution** is how often each value (or range of values) occurs. Summaries like the mean hide it; a **histogram** shows it by counting values in equal-width bins.
Each bin includes its left edge and excludes its right one, except the last, which includes both. Look at the shape before you trust any single number: one peak or two? Symmetric or a long tail?

steps.explain: Two bins: [0, 5) and [5, 10]. The values 0, 1, 1, 4 land in the first; 5, 5, 5 and 10 in the second (the last bin includes its right edge).

steps.title: Common shapes
body: A few shapes come up again and again, and NumPy's generator can draw from each:
rng.normal(loc=170, scale=8, size=1000)     # bell curve: heights, measurement errors
rng.uniform(0, 1, size=1000)                # flat: every value equally likely
For a **normal** distribution about 68% of values fall within 1 std of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.
A **right-skewed** distribution has a long tail of big values, which pulls the mean above the median. Incomes, prices and durations are usually right-skewed.

steps.prompt: A dataset has mean 52 and median 38. What shape is it most likely to have?
options: Right-skewed (a long tail of large values)
Left-skewed (a long tail of small values)
steps.explain: Large values in the tail pull the mean up past the median. Left skew is the opposite: mean below median.

steps.prompt: Which shape would you expect for each measurement?
items: Time until the next bus arrives
Repeated measurements of a table's length

steps.title: How much is within k standard deviations?
prompt: Write `share_within(x, k)` returning the fraction (a float between 0 and 1, rounded to 3 decimals) of values in `x` within `k` population standard deviations (`np.std(x)`) of the mean, inclusive.
The tests also draw 10,000 normal values and check you get close to the 68-95-99.7 rule.

import numpy as np


def share_within(x, k):

hints: `np.abs(x - x.mean()) <= k * x.std()` is a boolean array.
The mean of a boolean array is the fraction of `True` values.
template: Dojo.eq("everything is within 3 std here", 1.0, share_within([5, 6, 7], 3))
Dojo.check("about 68% within 1 std of a normal sample", 0.66 < _one < 0.70, f"got {_one}")

steps.title: z-scores
body: A **z-score** says how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean:

z-scores put different scales side by side: a test score with z = 2 is unusually high whatever the test's units were. A rough outlier rule for bell-shaped data is `abs(z) > 3`. (For skewed data prefer the IQR rule from the last lesson.)

steps.prompt: Draw a labelled histogram of the z-scores.

steps.title: z-scores and unusual values
prompt: - `zscores(x)`: the z-scores of `x` (population std), as a **list** of floats rounded to 2 decimals.
- `unusual(x, limit=2.0)`: the original values whose absolute z-score is greater than `limit`, as a list in their original order.
solution: return [v for v, zi in zip(x, z) if abs(zi) > limit]
hints: For `unusual`, zip the original values with their z-scores and keep those with `abs(z) > limit`.
template: Dojo.eq("a stricter limit finds nothing", [], unusual([10, 11, 9, 10, 12, 30], limit=3))

steps.title: Describe the shape
prompt: 1. draws a histogram of `x` with `plt.hist(x, bins=bins)`, x label `"value"`, y label `"count"` and title `"Distribution"`;
2. returns `"right-skewed"` if `mean - median > 0.1 * std`, `"left-skewed"` if `median - mean > 0.1 * std`, else `"symmetric"` (population std).
The tests try it on normal and exponential samples and look at the chart you drew.
